Q: I made this item stock management system i want you guys to critique this and tell me how can i get better A:

How can i write a code efficiently in less lines ?

This is a bad question. There's being succinct, and then there's being clear. Typically, succinct code is clearer to a point. And then it becomes deeply unclear. Strictly wanting less lines is bad.

You should want shorter, single-responsibility methods. Avoid being clever for cleverness's sake. You want clear APIs that don't require a lookup just to get a basic idea of what a method does. You can get some easy, succinct code by leveraging the Standard Library when it makes sense, and well regarded libraries.

You did ask for resources, so check out the good book list.

Q: What are optimal scrypt work factors? A:

Short answer

So that it takes 250 ms to verify a password

Long answer

The memory required for scrypt to operate is calculated as:

128 bytes × cost (N) × blockSizeFactor (r)

for the parameters you quote (N=16384, r=8, p=1)

128×16384×8 = 16,777,216 bytes = 16 MB

You have to take this into account when choosing parameters.

Bcrypt is "weaker" than Scrypt (although still three orders of magnitude stronger than PBKDF2) because it only requires 4 KB of memory. You want to make it difficult to parallelize cracking in hardware. For example, if a video card has 1.5 GB of on-board memory and you tuned scrypt to consume 1 GB of memory:

128×16384×512 = 1,073,741,824 bytes = 1 GB

then an attacker could not parallelize it on their video card. But then your application/phone/server would need to use 1 GB of RAM every time they calculated a password.

It helps me to think about the scrypt parameters as a rectangle. Where:

  • the width is the amount of memory required (128*N*r)
  • the height is the number of iterations performed
  • and the resulting area is the overall hardness

  • the cost (N) increases both memory usage and iterations.
  • the blockSizeFactor (r) increases memory usage.

The remaining parameter parallelization (p) means that you have to do the entire thing 2, 3, or more times:

If you had more memory than CPU, you could calculate the three separate paths in parallel - requiring triple the memory:

But in all real-world implementations, it is calculated in series, tripling the calculations needed:

In reality, nobody has ever chosen a p factor other than p=1.

What are the ideal factors?

  • As much RAM as you can spare
  • for as much time as you can spare!

  • scrypt is weaker than bcrypt for password storage if scrypt is configured to use less than 4 MB 1
  • Argon2 (i/d/id) is weaker than bcrypt when it comes to password hashing for authentication (i.e. <1,000 ms verification time) 2

Q: Bicubic, Bilinear, and Nearest-Neighbor Resampling for Image Resizing A:

A few important distinctions are missing here.

First, a practical image resize is usually implemented using inverse mapping, also called backward mapping.

You normally iterate over destination pixels, map each destination pixel center back into continuous source coordinates, then sample/filter the source image:

x_s = (x_d + 0.5) * W_s / W_d - 0.5
y_s = (y_d + 0.5) * H_s / H_d - 0.5

dst[x_d, y_d] = sample(src, x_s, y_s)

Mapping each source pixel forward to a destination pixel is not enough by itself. It can leave holes, because some destination pixels may receive no source sample, and it can create collisions, because several source pixels may map to the same destination pixel. Forward mapping can be used, but then it needs splatting, accumulation, or rasterization of the source pixel footprint.

Second, the choice of filter depends strongly on whether you are upsampling or downsampling.

For upsampling, the problem is mostly reconstruction/interpolation: how to estimate values between existing samples. Nearest, bilinear, bicubic, Catmull-Rom, B-spline, Mitchell-Netravali, Bell, and Lanczos are all possible tradeoffs between speed, sharpness, smoothness, and ringing.

For downsampling, the main issue is anti-aliasing. A single point sample with nearest, bilinear, or bicubic is often not enough. The filter footprint should usually grow with the reduction factor, otherwise high-frequency detail aliases instead of being properly averaged. Area/box filters, mipmaps, Gaussian pyramids, polyphase filters, and scale-aware Lanczos-style filters are common approaches.

So the list is not limited to nearest, bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos. Other common filters include box/area, triangle, Bell, B-spline, Catmull-Rom, Mitchell-Netravali, Gaussian, Hermite, and different Lanczos variants such as Lanczos2 or Lanczos3. They are not all interchangeable: some are interpolating filters, some are smoothing/reconstruction filters, and some are mainly useful for reduction.

There is also a performance dimension. A high-quality offline resize can afford a more expensive filter than a real-time video player, UI renderer, or game engine. CPU implementations often rely on separable passes, precomputed weights, SIMD/vectorization, cache-friendly tiling, multithreading, and multi-pass reduction for large downscales.

Finally, GPU-oriented filtering should be mentioned separately. Real-time rendering commonly uses nearest, bilinear, trilinear mipmap filtering, and anisotropic filtering because texture units accelerate those operations. Trilinear filtering blends between mipmap levels. Anisotropic filtering handles non-uniform or elongated source footprints, such as textured surfaces viewed at an oblique angle.

These methods are not GPU-only: they can be implemented on CPU too. But without hardware texture units, trilinear and especially anisotropic filtering can be expensive, so practical CPU implementations need careful optimization or approximations.

High-quality resampling also depends on details that are easy to overlook: boundary handling, alpha premultiplication, and ideally filtering in linear light rather than directly in gamma-encoded sRGB.
